newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Angry Argentina may take U.S. trade move to WTO.
newsitem.headline: Angry Argentina may take U.S. trade move to WTO.

text.p: The Argentine Economy Ministry said Wednesday it was "pretty annoyed" at the United States' withdrawal of Argentina's trade benefits and is looking into an appeal to the World Trade Organization.

Coordination Secretary Julio Caceres told reporters that the ministry believed Argentina's new patents legislation, the cause of the punitive measure signed by President Bill Clinton Tuesday, fully complied with WTO requirements.
Clinton signed an order slashing by 50 percent the number of Argentine goods than can be imported into the United States duty-free under the Generalized System of Preferences.
The U.S. president cited the country's "inadequate" intellectual property laws -- the subject of a long-running row between the two otherwise firm allies.
"The Economy Ministry is pretty annoyed by this measure they have taken when they are supposed to be the leaders in free trade," the official said.

Asked whether the government planned to act on Congress's request for a WTO appeal, Caceres said: "There is the option of putting it to international organisms that we are complying with the requirements of the WTO."
Argentine deputies in Congress's Industry Committee also want retaliatory measures, including the exclusion of U.S. firms from future privatization tenders.
But Caceres said it was "not convenient to take bilateral moves if we have international forums."

Washington has long urged Argentina to update intellectual property legislation, especially for pharmaceutical products. Until the new laws were introduced in 1995 and 1996, there was no restriction at all on copying foreign drug patents and U.S. drug firms said they lost $500 million a year to "piracy."
But Washington believes the new legislation still does not afford enough protection, and it takes special exception to the five-year transition period for patent protection.
